title: Muay Thai and kickboxing
note: Muay Thai, Thailand's national combat sport, is the art of eight limbs: fists, elbows, knees, and shins. Its distinctive tools are the teep, a push kick that controls distance, the shin roundhouse, and the clinch, where fighters control the head and strike with knees. Kickboxing rule sets usually narrow this arsenal.

read.title: Eight limbs and the clinch
text: Muay Thai earns its nickname, the art of eight limbs, by using fists, elbows, knees, and shins. A Western boxer stands bladed and low to slip punches; a Thai fighter usually stands taller and squarer, ready to lift a shin and check a low kick or answer with a knee.

The roundhouse kick lands with the shin rather than the foot. The fighter turns the hip over so that body weight swings through the leg like a bat. The teep, a push kick with the ball or sole of the foot, works more like a jab: it keeps an opponent at bay, interrupts combinations, and steals balance.

At close range the fight becomes standing grappling. In the clinch, fighters fight for inside position, often clasping both hands behind the opponent's head. Pulling the head down breaks posture and opens the way for knees, while sweeps and dumps can put an off-balance opponent on the canvas.
Many kickboxing rule sets trim this arsenal. K-1-style rules usually ban elbows and limit clinching, which pushes fighters toward punches and kicks at middle range.
